hook: Did you know the man who built Egypt's first stone pyramid was so brilliant he became a god?
article: Forty-seven hundred years ago, a commoner named Imhotep stepped into the court of Pharaoh Djoser and imagined something humanity had never seen. By stacking six limestone mastabas one above the other, he erected the Step Pyramid, the very first monumental stone structure in human history.

Yet Imhotep was far more than an architect, authoring the world's earliest surgical textbook two thousand years before Hippocrates was born. Instead of relying on superstition, he systematically documented forty-eight medical cases, prescribed honey for open wounds, and provided the first recorded description of the human brain.

He became one of only two mortals elevated to the ranks of full deities in the entire three-thousand-year history of ancient Egypt. To this day, the resting place of this master architect and healer has never been found, leaving his ultimate tomb hidden somewhere beneath the desert sands.
author: Wknight94 talk

hook: Imagine going out to look for a stray goat and accidentally dropping straight into a secret cavern of forty ancient kings.
article: In the summer of 1871, a local villager named Ahmed Abdel Rassoul slipped down a hidden cleft in the cliffs above Luxor. He dropped into a dark abyss smelling of ancient cedar and myrrh, striking a match to find himself face-to-face with the gilded faces of forty pharaohs.

For ten long years, the Abdel Rassoul family kept the tomb a total secret while cautiously selling small royal amulets and papyrus fragments on the black market. The astonishing discovery only came to light when priceless 21st Dynasty royal artifacts began flooding the antiquities trade in Europe.

Today, those very pharaohs rest in state at the National Museum of Egyptian Civilization in Cairo. You can explore Egypt's hidden historical caches through bespoke private archaeology expeditions and luxury travel.
author: Merja Attia
